extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of literature, rhetoric, and moral philosophy; general readers of The Spectator
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative principles for rhetoric, sermon-writing, poetry, and moral excellence as discussed in Addison's Spectator essays and accompanying motto translations. Focuses on what makes speech, writing, and character admirable or effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eloquence as the power of doctrine (Pauline model)
rubrics_metrics.description: St. Paul’s superiority in oratory is ascribed to the power of the doctrines he delivered; his sermons moved hearers as if they were the 'Voice of God' rather than merely human eloquence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the content and moral weight of what is preached (doctrine) to give speeches true persuasive force; consider St. Paul's harangues (e.g., at Lystra, Corinth, before Agrippa) as exemplary models for combining instruction and sublime rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lasting influence as a mark of true eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: An orator’s excellence may be judged by the visible marks and footsteps he leaves and by his becoming a standard to succeeding ages (e.g., Longinus's judgment of St. Paul).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate eloquence by its enduring effect and ability to set standards for later speakers, not merely by transient applause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt rhetorical method to the laws/venue
rubrics_metrics.description: In some contexts (e.g., Athens' courts) appeals to the affections and theatrical strokes of oratory were forbidden; therefore strict argument alone was required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conform rhetorical technique to the conventions and legal/audience constraints of the venue — where emotional appeals are inappropriate or forbidden, rely on strict argumentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate balance of argument and appeals to the affections
rubrics_metrics.description: Different discourses call for different emphases: strict argument in legal settings; more moving, affective rhetoric in sermons or exhortations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose whether to aim at reason or feeling depending on purpose and audience; misuse (e.g., unnecessary ornament in a place needing argument) is an anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sermons should combine instruction with rhetorical excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Clergy may learn from St. Paul's harangues that, beyond being instructive, sermons can receive a great addition from skilful oratory and the power of their doctrines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing sermons, aim both for sound instruction and for a style that can move and persuade — use examples of scriptural speeches as practical models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral greatness: suppression of desires and patient self-command
rubrics_metrics.description: The virtuous ideal is one who arms himself with patience, suppresses passions and desires, has few wants, and cherishes virtues — described as making men 'like gods' in the best philosophical sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess moral excellence by the degree of self-mastery, modest desires, and the habitual practice of virtuous acts toward others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate the right exemplar (divine as pattern for virtue)
rubrics_metrics.description: Revealed religion provides a more just and perfect idea of the Supreme Being, which supplies a proper object for imitation; choosing the right model (God) is crucial for moral refinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When proposing models for moral behavior or character, prefer exemplars whose motives and ends are fitting (i.e., imitate use of understanding and benevolence rather than vice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound judgment as the foundation of good writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct quotation/translation: 'Sound judgment is the ground of writing well.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize clear, sensible judgment about what to include, tone, and structure; good taste and critical sense underlie effective prose or verse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthful sentiment and well-wrought character over ornate artifice
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted maxim: 'When the sentiments and manners please, and all the characters are wrought with ease, your tale, though void of beauty, force, and art, more strongly shall delight ... Than where a lifeless pomp of verse appears.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value authentic emotion and natural depiction of character over artificial ornamentation; a simple but truthful tale can beat elaborate but lifeless style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid incoherent, miscellaneous style (unity and coherence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Horace's admonition against incoherent style that 'varies all shapes, and mixes all extremes' — such a book is ridiculous like a malformed picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain unity of style and coherence of parts; don't mix incompatible modes, tones, or genres in ways that confuse the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry and prose should paint vivid images ('poems like pictures')
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted: 'Poems like pictures are.' (Hor. Ars Poet.), implying that literary work should present clear, image-rich scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for evocative imagery and concrete detail that allow readers to 'see' the scene; visual clarity strengthens emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good taste aligns with nature (naturalness as criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted: 'Good taste and nature always speak the same.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate style and content by whether they accord with natural feeling and common sense rather than artificial fashions; naturalness is a sign of good taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance outweighs superficial applause or pomp
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrated by translations mocking applause for costume/wig rather than for actual speech (e.g., stage applause at Booth's entrance despite no speech): true merit is not measured by noisy acclaim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge work by intrinsic qualities (argument, character, feeling), not by ephemeral popular display or ceremonious applause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate intellectual faculties and curiosity for higher excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice that a generous ambition to 'improve my faculties' and cultivate contemplation prepares one for higher discovery and 'exalted station' in the life to come.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage sustained intellectual development — study, curiosity, and contemplation are practical means to produce higher-quality thought and writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation of attachment: not being over-addicted to any one thing
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted rule of life: 'not to be too much addicted to any one thing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess personal character and conduct by the virtue of moderation and balance; extreme single-mindedness is a fault.
